Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Agyinasare demands full disclosure of National Cathedral money Source : Myjoyonline.com 17 November 2026 5:25am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Archbishop Charles Agyinasare has challenged those behind the National Cathedral project to open their financial records to public scrutiny, insisting that churches must know how contributions have been handled before being asked to help complete the controversial facility.
He said any attempt to revive the project without first accounting for the money raised and spent would be premature, particularly given the questions surrounding the reported cost of the construction so far.
The Founder and Prelate of Perez Chapel International said the first step should be to establish how much had come into the project, how much had been expended and what remained outstanding.
“Let’s see what the account says first. And then when we see what the account says then we can know, because I know churches and us contributed some monies but we don’t know what the account is,” he said.
He expressed concern about the reported GH¢97 million expenditure, saying he wanted to examine the accounts before supporting any proposal for the churches to take over the project.
“If it’s true that GHC97 million was spent and that’s what we have, it’s a problem. And so I would wish that I could see the accounts,” he stated in an interview on Channel One TV on Monday, November 16, 2026.
Archbishop Agyinasare disclosed that some churches, including his own, had made financial contributions towards the project but had not been given sufficient information about how the funds were accounted for.
He said the financial position must be made clear before churches could determine whether they were willing and able to assume responsibility for completing the facility.
Archbishop Agyinasare said the political divisions surrounding the cathedral should not be allowed to prevent an objective assessment of its future.
“I think that the politics of it is a problem and we should move past the politics of it and then pick it up from there,” he said.
Archbishop Charles Agyinasare wants cathedral retained for national use
Despite his reservations about the project's finances, the archbishop said the site should not be abandoned, arguing that the substantial work already undertaken there should be considered in deciding its future.
He proposed that the facility could be developed into a venue for important national events, including presidential swearing-in ceremonies and other major indoor state functions.
He said such a use would give the project a broader national purpose beyond the original personal pledge that inspired its construction.
The cathedral project was initiated under former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, who proposed the construction of a national worship centre and made a personal pledge towards it. The project subsequently became the subject of intense public debate over its financing, cost and management.
In July 2025, the government disclosed findings from a Deloitte and Touche audit of the National Cathedral Secretariat covering 2021 to 2023. The report identified procurement breaches, questionable payments, weaknesses in financial controls and discrepancies in consultancy fees.
One finding was an unexplained difference of about GH¢4.93 million between the amount the Office of the President recorded as paid to Sir David Adjaye & Associates and the amount the firm reported receiving.
The government also disclosed that the total financial commitment to the project had reached US$97 million, comprising US$58 million already paid or committed and a further US$39 million outstanding to the contractor. It subsequently ordered a forensic audit to examine the project more comprehensively.
In October 2026, the Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, announced that the construction site had been handed back to the government while the Attorney-General reviewed the forensic audit.
The minister also confirmed that the Board of Trustees had been dissolved and that the government would not commit further public funds to the construction.
The government's position is that the next steps will be determined after the Attorney-General's advice on the audit.
Archbishop Agyinasare's intervention adds to the debate over whether the project should be completed through contributions from churches, repurposed for wider national use or subjected to a different arrangement.
